title: AMLA Executive Board Member Derville Rowland speaks at AFME’s European AML Conference

paras.text: Rowland described AMLA as a redesign of how the EU AML/CFT system operates, rather than simply new rules or another European institution. She presented AMLA’s ambition for a system that works as one: unified, risk-based and technologically advanced, and focused on outcomes rather than processes. Through its roles in supervision, regulation and FIU coordination, AMLA aims to strengthen the EU's ability anticipate, deter and disrupt financial crime, while reinforcing confidence in the integrity of the Single Market.
She outlined how AMLA is turning this ambition into reality across three connected areas:
Direct supervision: from 2028, AMLA will directly supervise up to 40 selected cross-border financial institutions or groups, with the first selection taking place in 2027.
Indirect supervision: national supervision of all other institutions will increasingly operate within a common European framework, supported by common methodologies and convergence tools.
Non-financial sector: AMLA will promote greater consistency and effectiveness across a diverse range of supervisory arrangements.

Rowland underlined that proportionality is central to this approach: the aim is consistency in supervisory outcomes, not uniformity for its own sake. She also highlighted technology and data as essential enablers of more targeted and effective supervision.
Speaking to the financial sector, she pointed to three key implications of the new framework:
Greater clarity and consistency , with clearer expectations and a more predictable supervisory environment for firms operating across borders.
A stronger focus on risk and effectiveness , directing resources where they make the greatest difference.
Preparation and engagement , encouraging institutions to prepare early for the application of the AML Regulation from 10 July 2027 and to engage actively in AMLA’s consultations.

Looking ahead, Rowland emphasised that AMLA will hold itself to the same standard of effectiveness it expects from institutions. She concluded that AMLA is not about more supervision, but better supervision, built on a genuine partnership between the EU and national authorities, FIUs and the financial sector.
